evals.prompt: I run Cablewright, a consumer-electronics accessories store. Our AOV is $180, gross margin is 24%, and variable costs run $16 per order (shipping, pick-pack, card fees). Returns are about 7%. Our catalog goes from $12 USB cables to $420 docking stations. I was looking at a couple of skincare affiliate programs paying 20% and I want to match that so affiliates actually take us seriously. Set our affiliate rate at 20% of order value and tell me how to pitch it.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to set 20%, with the contribution-margin walk computed from the given numbers, a derived single-digit ceiling, a per-order loss figure for the 20% proposal, and a fix for the wide catalog spread.
expectations: Rejects the 20% rate and states it sits above the ceiling derived from this store's own unit economics
Computes gross margin per order as about $43.20 from the $180 AOV at 24%
Subtracts the $16 variable cost to reach a contribution margin of about $27.20
Nets out the 7% return rate to reach a post-return contribution margin of about $25.30
Applies the one-third-to-one-half-of-post-return-contribution-margin rule to set the payable band
States a maximum payable per order of roughly $12.65, i.e. a ceiling around 7% of AOV
Quantifies the loss at 20%: about $36 paid against about $25.30 of post-return contribution, roughly $11 lost per order
Cross-checks the derived figure against the 20-30%-of-gross-margin sanity band
Recommends a headline rate in the single digits (roughly 4-7%), or an equivalent flat CPA, rather than a double-digit rate
Flags that a flat percentage across a $12-to-$420 catalog lets one large order wipe out unit economics, and offers flat CPA or a percentage banded by product as the fix
States that the loss would be invisible at launch and surface only after returns net out
Names narrowing the program to high-margin SKUs as the fallback if partners will not work at the derived rate, and does not justify any rate by pointing at the skincare vertical's benchmark

evals.prompt: Stackline Ops here, B2B SaaS. Our $89/mo plan carries 84% gross margin and monthly churn is about 3.3%, so customers stick around roughly 30 months. Today we pay affiliates 25% recurring for the life of the account and our CFO says it is way out of line. Our CEO's fix is to drop the headline to 12% but keep it lifetime so we don't lose the recruiting story. Run the numbers and tell us whether to go to 12%.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to change the duration rule before the headline, with lifetime, capped and tapered costs computed against the $2,670 LTV, both ceiling legs checked, and the 12% lifetime proposal rejected.
expectations: Recommends fixing the recurring duration rule before touching the headline percentage
States explicitly that the duration rule moves effective cost far more than the headline percentage does
Computes the current lifetime cost at roughly $667 per customer (25% of $89 over about 30 months)
Computes a 12-month cap at the unchanged 25% headline at about $267 per customer
Shows the 12-month cap at 25% costs less than the proposed 12% lifetime (about $320 per customer)
Recommends against the 12% lifetime proposal
Expresses total commission per customer as a share of the roughly $2,670 revenue LTV and checks it against the 5-15% band
Checks total commission per customer against the 30-40%-of-gross-margin ceiling as a separate condition
Notes that keeping the 25% headline protects recruiting pull, because partners weigh headline and duration together
Offers a taper (25% for months 1-6, a lower rate for months 7-12) as the lower-cost alternative and states its cost
Notes the taper needs a second rate step the affiliate platform may not express, and names the plain 12-month cap or a renewal bonus as the fallback when it cannot
Proposes a renewal bonus in the 5-10% range as the way to keep partners engaged past the cap rather than extending the rate

evals.prompt: Cratefox, inventory software for small warehouses. $129/mo, 61% gross margin, monthly churn is 7.5% so average tenure is around 13 months. Two competitors advertise lifetime recurring commissions and three of our better affiliates have moved to them in the last two months. Price me a lifetime option and a 12-month option side by side so I can decide which one to publish.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to price lifetime for these numbers, naming the three conditions and which ones fail, plus a capped structure with a renewal bonus as the competitive answer.
expectations: Refuses to price a lifetime commission option for this program
Names the three conditions lifetime requires: gross margin above roughly 80%, monthly churn below roughly 5%, and competing programs already paying lifetime
Identifies the 61% gross margin as failing the margin condition
Identifies the 7.5% monthly churn as failing the churn condition
States that competitors paying lifetime is not on its own sufficient to qualify the option
Does not present lifetime anywhere in the answer as the more generous alternative to compare against the capped option
Recommends a 12-month cap as the default duration rule
Offers a renewal bonus of roughly 5-10% of renewal value as the way to compete on perceived generosity without open-ended liability
Explains the liability: on a sticky product, a long-tenured customer can earn an affiliate more than that customer's margin
Notes that published lifetime terms are expensive to retract later because of network decrease rules and grandfathering obligations
Recommends paying recurring commission in arrears on confirmed billing events so churned customers stop costing automatically

evals.prompt: Lunepeak, DTC haircare. Everyone in our affiliate program is on a flat 15% of order value. Two large cashback sites now account for 38% of our affiliate revenue and I am fairly sure most of those buyers were already coming to us. I asked our affiliate platform vendor about tagging new customers versus repeat customers and they said it is not on their roadmap this year. Give me a plan to stop overpaying those two without killing the relationship.
evals.expected_output: A control plan led by a rate cap rather than a new-customer gate, with differentiated windows, incrementality figures, and a holdout test with both read rules.
expectations: Does not recommend a new-customer gate as an action to take now, given the tracking limitation
Names capping the cashback rate below the content/creator rate as the first control to apply
Places the rate cap ahead of shortening the attribution window in the recommended order
Recommends a shorter attribution window for the cashback partners than for content partners
Gives a concrete short window for the cashback partners in the 24-hour-to-7-day range
States that coupon, cashback and loyalty partners commonly run substantially non-incremental, on the order of two-thirds of attributed volume
States that content and creator partners run largely incremental, on the order of 80%
Prescribes a 30-day holdout test on the top cashback partners
States the holdout read rule: flat total conversion volume with falling affiliate-attributed volume means the partners were harvesting existing demand, so keep their rates capped
States the opposite holdout read rule: a drop in total volume means they were incremental, so restore their rates and document it
Recommends exclusive per-partner codes as the control that produces evidence rather than only savings, while naming its ongoing reconciliation cost
Notes the new-customer gate becomes the first control to apply once the tracking flag ships

evals.prompt: Formwork Analytics. We are launching an affiliate program in six weeks, nothing live yet, zero affiliates signed. I want a three-tier bronze/silver/gold commission ladder from day one because it gives the recruiting pitch something to aim at. Give me the three rates and the conversion breakpoints between them.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to set breakpoints without performance history, a flat launch rate with a stated revisit condition, and the tier mechanics for when tiers do arrive.
expectations: Declines to set tier breakpoints for a program with no historical partner performance data
States the reason: with no performance history there is nowhere to place a breakpoint
Recommends launching with a single flat rate
Gives a concrete condition or timeframe that triggers revisiting tiers later
Does not present a bronze/silver/gold ladder with invented thresholds as the recommendation
Explains that once history exists, the first tier should be reachable by roughly 70-80% of active partners
States the top tier should be reserved for roughly the top 10-20% of partners
Recommends marginal tiers over retroactive tiers when tiers are eventually introduced
Explains that retroactive tiers reprice a partner's whole period, making program cost unforecastable rather than merely higher
Explains the cliff incentive: a partner just short of a breakpoint is pushed to add low-quality sign-ups
Recommends new-customer revenue as the tier threshold metric ahead of gross revenue or referral count

evals.prompt: Beltram Goods, DTC cookware. Our affiliate terms today are a 60-day validation hold, net-45 payment, and a $250 minimum payout threshold. Three mid-size affiliates left for a competitor last quarter and two of them said cash flow was the reason. My plan is to cut the validation hold from 60 days to 10 so money moves faster. Sanity-check that and write the new payout terms.
evals.expected_output: A reordered set of payout-speed levers putting the threshold first and validation last, with the reversibility risk of a short validation window stated and validation tied to the return window.
expectations: Recommends lowering the $250 minimum threshold before shortening the validation window
Gives a concrete replacement threshold in the $50-100 range
States that lowering the threshold adds no risk because the money is owed to the partner either way
Recommends shortening net terms toward net-30 ahead of touching validation
Places shortening the validation window last among the three levers
Conditions any validation cut on first measuring the reversal or refund rate and finding it low
Explains that a shortened validation window pays commissions before refunds and chargebacks land
Explains that a commission already paid comes back only through a manual clawback
Notes that validation and net terms stack, and that the stack is what produces the wait affiliates feel
Quantifies the current end-to-end wait as roughly three to four months
Notes the minimum threshold is the lever the smallest and newest partners feel first
Ties the validation period length to the product's return or refund window rather than to an arbitrary figure

evals.prompt: Verdantly, garden supplies. We run a live program on a major affiliate network with 340 approved affiliates, everyone on a flat 14% of order value. I want to move to 7% for cashback and deal sites and 12% for content sites, effective next Monday, announced in one email blast to the whole base. Write the announcement email and the rollout plan.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the next-Monday single-blast plan, citing the network's contractual decrease caps, a multi-step sequenced cut, 60 days' notice, grandfathering and top-partner-first phasing.
expectations: Flags that the affiliate network contractually caps the size, frequency and notice period of a commission decrease
States the published rule shape: at most a 20% reduction per change, no more than once every 30 days, with at least 7 days' partner notice
Identifies 14% to 7% as a 50% cut, too large to make in a single step under that rule
Sequences the reduction into multiple steps spaced at least 30 days apart
Recommends roughly 60 days' notice for the change, ahead of the network's minimum
Rejects the next-Monday effective date and the single all-base email blast
Recommends grandfathering existing affiliates at the old rate, holding high performers for at least one cycle
Recommends phasing the rollout top-partners-first, with direct conversations before any broadcast
Recommends leading the announcement with what stays the same
Requires deriving the 7% and 12% target rates from unit economics before announcing them, rather than migrating to chosen-by-feel numbers
Notes that adding a partner-type rate row carries less contractual exposure than cutting an existing published rate
Names silent or abrupt rate changes as a known cause of partner churn

evals.prompt: Nordholt Tools, B2B. We derived our affiliate ceiling at 14% of first-year contract value and the program launches in five weeks to line up with a trade show. ToolBench Review, the biggest review site in our category, told us flat out they do not do performance-only deals. They want $9,000 per quarter as a placement fee plus 8% commission on what they refer. Since 8% is well under our 14% ceiling this looks like a bargain to me. Should we sign, and how do I fit it into the rate card?
evals.expected_output: A correction that the placement fee sits outside the derived ceiling, a recommendation to launch on straight percentage given the five-week date, and the hybrid pursued separately with its effort and contract costs named.
expectations: States explicitly that the $9,000 placement fee sits outside the commission ceiling derived from unit economics
Explains why: the fee is paid before any conversion, so the ceiling derivation does not bound it
Rejects the user's reasoning that 8% being under the 14% ceiling makes the deal inherently affordable
Notes that hybrid is the only model that lands a publisher refusing pure performance
Names the effort cost: a negotiation per partner plus off-platform invoicing and reconciliation every cycle
Flags that the five-week hard date does not accommodate a hybrid negotiation
Recommends launching on a straight percentage-of-revenue model and pursuing the publisher deal on a separate track
Keeps percentage of revenue as the default rate model for the rest of the partner base
Requires the placement fee to be budgeted and reported separately from commission cost
Requires a fixed contract term for the placement fee rather than an open-ended arrangement
Does not present hybrid as the generally superior or most generous of the three rate models
Offers a milestone bonus tied to new-customer revenue as a lower-commitment instrument to test this publisher first

evals.prompt: Sablefin, B2B SaaS. $199/mo, 79% gross margin, average tenure 20 months, blended CAC $740. We pay 20% recurring capped at 12 months. We have 412 approved affiliates but only 11 of them produced a single conversion last quarter, and affiliate revenue has been flat three quarters running. Competitors advertise 30%. I want to go to 35% to leapfrog them. Write up the new rate and the announcement.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that activation is the binding problem, a rejection of 35% on the LTV leg of the ceiling, and top-partner instruments instead of a public headline increase.
expectations: Identifies partner activation rather than rate level as the likely root cause, given 11 converting affiliates out of 412
States that a correctly derived commission structure does not rescue a program nobody promotes
Points the user toward recruitment, onboarding or activation work as the primary fix
Computes the cost of the proposed 35% capped at 12 months at roughly $836 per customer
Compares that figure against the roughly $3,980 revenue LTV and shows it exceeds the 5-15%-of-LTV band
Recommends against raising the public headline to 35%
Checks total commission per customer against the 30-40%-of-gross-margin ceiling as a second, separate condition
States that both conditions must hold, not either one on its own
Notes that a small share of affiliates produces most program revenue, so the rate card should be designed for the head rather than the long tail
Recommends custom or private rates for a handful of top partners instead of raising the public headline for everyone
Names a milestone bonus tied to new-customer revenue as a top-partner instrument that cannot exceed the ceiling by surprise
Recommends checking projected cost per incremental affiliate-acquired customer against the $740 blended CAC

evals.prompt: Halcombe Labs. Just give me the right commission rate for a B2B SaaS affiliate program. I keep seeing 20-30% quoted everywhere and I do not want to overthink this - we launch in three weeks and I need a number for the landing page today.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to name a rate before collecting the economic inputs, delivered as a one-question-at-a-time interview covering margin, churn, LTV/CAC, deadline, mandate and platform capability.
expectations: Does not state a recommended commission rate before collecting economic inputs
Asks for gross margin
Asks for monthly churn rate or average customer tenure
Asks for customer LTV and current or target blended CAC
Asks one question per message rather than presenting the whole questionnaire at once
Offers multiple-choice answer options where the question allows it
Accepts estimates rather than exact figures, while insisting on some number before proposing a rate
Asks whether this is a one-off fix or a rate card meant to survive several years of plan changes
Asks what the affiliate platform can actually express and who administers the program week to week
Treats the 20-30% figures the user has seen as calibration to apply after deriving, never as the answer itself

evals.prompt: Pellwood Home, ecommerce. Six months into our affiliate program we paid out $86,000 including network fees and got 2,900 attributed orders, so $29.66 per order against a blended CAC of $41. That is 28% cheaper than our other channels, so I want to go to the board and ask to double the affiliate budget. About 46% of that order volume comes from two cashback partners and a coupon aggregator, the rest from content sites and creators. Check my math before I present it.
evals.expected_output: A recomputation with the denominator discounted by incrementality, showing the program fails the below-CAC leg, plus the ranked fixes with the coupon split first and the headline cut last.
expectations: Recomputes cost per acquired customer with the denominator discounted by incrementality rather than using raw attributed orders
Applies a low incrementality share to the coupon and cashback volume, on the order of one-third
Applies a high incrementality share to the content and creator volume, on the order of 80%
Produces an incrementality-adjusted cost per customer materially above the raw $29.66 figure, in the neighbourhood of $50
Concludes the program fails the below-CAC leg of the pass threshold once incrementality is applied
Names the failure mode: a program can appear to beat CAC on paper while buying demand it already had
Applies the second leg of the pass threshold as well, checking total commission against the derived margin ceiling
States that both legs must hold for the structure to pass
Names rebalancing the partner-type split as the highest-value fix here, because the overpayment is concentrated in coupon and cashback volume
Places cutting the headline rate last among the fixes
Does not offer a recurring-duration or taper lever, since this is a one-shot per-order ecommerce program
Prescribes a 30-day holdout on the top coupon and cashback partners to confirm the incrementality assumption rather than leaving it as an estimate
